title: Join two boards end to end on three dowels
instruction: Join the two boards on the three dowels so that their ends meet, flat on the bench, then let go.
context: Wooden dowels hold most flat-pack furniture together: a bookcase or a wardrobe arrives as panels with rows of holes and a bag of 8 mm dowels, and whoever puts it up at home pushes each panel onto the dowels standing in the next. Nearly everyone has done it or watched it done, and knows how it goes wrong: several dowels must find their holes at once, with about a tenth of a millimetre to spare, and a part pushed on a little askew jams on the first dowel and stops. Here the same joint is made dry with two short boards on three dowels. Each board lies beside its own arm and neither arm reaches the other board, so the joint is made by two hands. Hands that both hold their board fast often leave the dowels standing at the holes' mouths; a practised assembler holds one part still and pushes the other home, so that it finds the dowels' line by itself.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x away from the arms, y to the left); heights over the bench top. One fixed layout, nothing varies by seed. Bench: a waxed laminate top (friction about 0.25 against wood). A cherry board, red-brown, 18 x 80 x 150 mm, 125 g, lying flat with its middle at x 36, y -33, long axis along y. Glued into its end that faces the midline, three beech dowel pins 8 x 40 mm with chamfered ends, 20 mm of each standing out, at 25 mm pitch on the end's centre line, 9 mm over the bench. A walnut board, dark brown, 18 x 80 x 150 mm, 140 g, lying flat with its middle at x 36, y +33, long axis along y; in its end that faces the midline three sockets drilled with an 8 mm brad-point bit, 22 mm deep, at the same pitch and height. The two ends are 51 cm apart. Nothing clamps, guides or stops either board. Both arms start in their ready pose.
scoring: Only the state at the end of the trial counts. The seam: the two openings between the boards' facing ends, at their two corners. Every level needs both openings not under -2 mm (the boards do not overlap), the boards within 2 mm of the same height and both flat within 3 degrees (a board lying on the other scores 0). 0.25: both openings 19 mm or less (the dowels' tips are in), the long edges in line within 1 mm and the boards square within 2 degrees. 0.5: both openings 10 mm or less. 0.75: both openings 0.5 mm or less and the long edges flush within 1 mm. 1.0: also both grippers 3 cm or more from both boards and everything at rest; held for 1 s the trial ends as a success. Real bench: a tape at the two corners for the first two levels; a 0.5 mm feeler gauge that enters neither corner and a straightedge along a long edge and across the two top faces for the closed joint; the video for the release.
reset_notes: Pull the boards apart by hand and lay them back on their marks, ends facing; check that no dowel is loose or bruised and blow the sockets clear. The trial is a dry fit: no glue.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at true size; the dowels are part of the cherry board. Each socket is a 24-sided bore 8.2 mm across (real: 8.0 to 8.1 mm), up to 0.1 mm a side looser than real. A dry fit: no glue or press fit. Friction 0.25 and the 1 mm chamfer are assumed. With both boards gripped the dowels went in once and stood at the mouths twice; the reference holds one board and pushes the other. In the top camera a seam of 8 mm cannot be told from a closed one.
